solution:
A carbinol carbon (the carbon bearing \(-\text{OH}\)) attached to one, two or three other carbon atoms makes the alcohol primary, secondary or tertiary respectively.
(i) \((\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\): the \(-\text{OH}\) carbon carries two H and one carbon — **primary**.
(ii) \(\text{H}_2\text{C}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\): the \(-\text{OH}\) carbon carries two H and one carbon — **primary** (allylic).
(iii) \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\): **primary**.
(iv) \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{CH}(\text{OH})-\text{CH}_3\): the \(-\text{OH}\) carbon is bonded to two carbons — **secondary** (benzylic).
(v) \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}(\text{OH})-\text{CH}_3\): two carbons on the carbinol carbon — **secondary**.
(vi) \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_2-\text{OH}\): the \(-\text{OH}\) carbon is bonded to three carbons — **tertiary** (allylic).

Primary: (i), (ii), (iii); Secondary: (iv), (v); Tertiary: (vi).

An allylic alcohol has its \(-\text{OH}\) group on an \(sp^3\) carbon that is directly attached to a carbon of a \(\text{C}=\text{C}\) double bond.
(ii) \(\text{H}_2\text{C}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\) — the carbinol carbon is next to the double bond (a primary allylic alcohol).
(vi) \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_2-\text{OH}\) — the carbinol carbon is next to the double bond (a tertiary allylic alcohol).
Compounds (iv) and (v) are benzylic, not allylic, because their carbinol carbon is attached to an aromatic ring rather than to an alkene carbon.

Allylic alcohols: (ii) and (vi).

[Textbook answer-key error in part (i): the key names the compound 4-chloro-3-ethyl-2-(1-methylethyl)butan-1-ol, using a FOUR-carbon parent chain. The principal chain must be the longest one containing the carbon that bears the \(-\text{OH}\), and a five-carbon chain running through the group the key itself calls "3-ethyl" does contain it — so the correct name is 3-(chloromethyl)-2-(propan-2-yl)pentan-1-ol. The book corroborates this against itself: the exercise key's answer to Ex 7.2(x) draws this same skeleton and takes the five-carbon chain as the parent. Part (ii) agrees.] The parent chain is the longest chain that contains the carbon bearing \(-\text{OH}\), and \(-\text{OH}\) gets the lowest possible locant.
(i) The longest chain through the carbinol carbon is five carbons (pentan-1-ol); C-2 carries a propan-2-yl group and C-3 a chloromethyl group: **3-(Chloromethyl)-2-(propan-2-yl)pentan-1-ol** (i.e. 3-chloromethyl-2-isopropylpentan-1-ol).
(ii) The chain chosen must contain both \(-\text{OH}\) groups; it is six carbons long with \(-\text{OH}\) at C-1 and C-3 and methyl groups at C-2 and C-5: **2,5-Dimethylhexane-1,3-diol**.
(iii) **3-Bromocyclohexan-1-ol**.
(iv) Six-carbon chain, double bond between C-1 and C-2, \(-\text{OH}\) at C-3: **Hex-1-en-3-ol**.
(v) Four-carbon chain from the \(\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\) carbon, double bond between C-2 and C-3: **2-Bromo-3-methylbut-2-en-1-ol**.

A Grignard reagent adds to the carbonyl carbon of methanal, and hydrolysis of the adduct gives a **primary** alcohol \(\text{RCH}_2\text{OH}\). So R must be the group attached to the \(-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\) carbon.
(i) For \((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\), R = propan-2-yl:
\((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}-\text{MgBr} + \text{HCHO} \rightarrow (\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2\text{OMgBr}\)
\((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2\text{OMgBr} \xrightarrow{\text{H}_3\text{O}^+} (\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2\text{OH} + \text{Mg(OH)Br}\)
(ii) For cyclohexylmethanol, R = cyclohexyl:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}-\text{MgBr} + \text{HCHO} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}-\text{CH}_2\text{OMgBr} \xrightarrow{\text{H}_3\text{O}^+} \text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\)

Reagents: 2-bromopropane/Mg and bromocyclohexane/Mg respectively, each treated with methanal and then hydrolysed.

(i) Acid-catalysed hydration follows Markovnikov's rule, the proton adding to the carbon carrying more hydrogen so that the more stable secondary carbocation is formed:
\(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{\text{H}^+} \text{CH}_3-\text{CH}(\text{OH})-\text{CH}_3\) — propan-2-ol.
(ii) \(\text{NaBH}_4\) is a mild hydride donor: it reduces the ketone carbonyl but leaves the ester group untouched. The ring \(\text{C}=\text{O}\) becomes \(\text{CH}-\text{OH}\), giving methyl 2-(2-hydroxycyclohexyl)acetate, i.e. a cyclohexane ring bearing \(-\text{OH}\) and, on the adjacent carbon, \(-\text{CH}_2\text{COOCH}_3\).
(iii) \(\text{NaBH}_4\) reduces the aldehyde to the corresponding primary alcohol:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CHO} \xrightarrow{\text{NaBH}_4} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\) — 2-methylbutan-1-ol.

All three reagents replace \(-\text{OH}\) by a halogen through cleavage of the C\(-\)O bond.

(i) Butan-1-ol (a primary alcohol):
(a) \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH} + \text{HCl} \xrightarrow{\text{ZnCl}_2} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}\) (1-chlorobutane) — slow, needs heating, so no turbidity at room temperature in the Lucas test.
(b) \(+\,\text{HBr} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}\) (1-bromobutane).
(c) \(+\,\text{SOCl}_2 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl} + \text{SO}_2 + \text{HCl}\) (1-chlorobutane).

(ii) 2-Methylbutan-2-ol (a tertiary alcohol):
(a) \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{OH} + \text{HCl} \xrightarrow{\text{ZnCl}_2} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{Cl}\) (2-chloro-2-methylbutane) — immediate turbidity, because a stable tertiary carbocation forms readily.
(b) \(+\,\text{HBr} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{Br}\) (2-bromo-2-methylbutane).
(c) \(+\,\text{SOCl}_2 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{Cl} + \text{SO}_2 + \text{HCl}\) (2-chloro-2-methylbutane).

Acid-catalysed dehydration removes \(-\text{OH}\) and a hydrogen from the adjacent carbon; where a choice exists the more highly substituted (more stable) alkene is the major product (Saytzeff rule).
(i) 1-Methylcyclohexanol is tertiary; loss of water gives a tertiary carbocation on the ring carbon, and loss of a proton from a ring carbon next to it gives the tetrasubstituted alkene:
major product **1-methylcyclohexene** (not methylenecyclohexane, which is only disubstituted).
(ii) Butan-1-ol is primary, so the protonated alcohol cannot lose water to a free primary carbocation — that intermediate is far too unstable. Instead water leaves with a concerted 1,2-hydride shift from C-2, giving the secondary (\(\text{sec}\)-butyl) cation. Loss of a proton from C-3 then gives the more highly substituted alkene, so the major product is **but-2-ene**:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}\text{CH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)
_note: For (ii) I have given but-1-ene, the direct elimination product of a primary alcohol. Under strongly acidic conditions the initially formed alkene can isomerise (or the primary carbocation can rearrange by a hydride shift) to but-2-ene, which is the thermodynamically more stable, more substituted alkene. If the key gives but-2-ene, the difference is one of pathway (E2 versus E1-with-rearrangement), not an arithmetic error.

solution:
In the phenoxide ion the negative charge on oxygen is delocalised into the ring, appearing on the ortho and para carbons:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^- \leftrightarrow\) structures with the negative charge on O, on the two ortho carbons and on the para carbon (five canonical structures in all).

When a \(-\text{NO}_2\) group occupies an ortho or a para position, the charge that resonance places on that very carbon can be pushed one step further, on to the oxygen atoms of the nitro group:

For o-nitrophenoxide: \(\text{O}^-\) on the ring oxygen \(\leftrightarrow\) charge on C-2 (the carbon bearing \(-\text{NO}_2\)) \(\leftrightarrow\) charge delocalised on to the nitro oxygens, \(-\text{N}^+(\text{O}^-)=\text{O} \rightarrow -\text{N}^+(\text{O}^-)-\text{O}^-\).
For p-nitrophenoxide: the same extended delocalisation operates from C-4.

The extra canonical structures put the negative charge on the highly electronegative oxygen atoms of the nitro group, so the phenoxide ion is far better stabilised. This is why ortho and para nitrophenols are more acidic than phenol itself, and why the meta isomer (whose \(-\text{NO}_2\) is not conjugated with the charge-bearing carbons) is much less strongly affected.

(i) **Reimer-Tiemann reaction.** Chloroform in aqueous alkali generates dichlorocarbene, \(:\text{CCl}_2\), which is the electrophile; the electron-rich phenoxide ion attacks it at the ortho position, and the substituted benzal chloride so formed is hydrolysed by the alkali:
\(\text{CHCl}_3 + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow :\text{CCl}_2 + \text{NaCl} + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} \xrightarrow{\text{CHCl}_3 + \text{aq. NaOH}} o\text{-HO-C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{CHCl}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{NaOH}} o\text{-HO-C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{CHO}\)
After acidification the product is salicylaldehyde (2-hydroxybenzaldehyde).

(ii) **Kolbe's reaction.** Phenol is first converted to the phenoxide ion, which is a stronger nucleophile than phenol itself; carbon dioxide, a weak electrophile, then attacks the ortho position:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{ONa} + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{ONa} \xrightarrow{\text{CO}_2} o\text{-HO-C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{COONa} \xrightarrow{\text{H}^+} o\text{-HO-C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{COOH}\)
The product is salicylic acid (2-hydroxybenzoic acid).

The target, 2-ethoxy-3-methylpentane, is \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}(\text{OC}_2\text{H}_5)-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3\). Williamson synthesis is an \(\text{S}_\text{N}2\) reaction, so the alkyl halide must be **primary**; the branched, secondary carbon must therefore come from the alkoxide.

Step 1 — make the halide from ethanol:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH} \xrightarrow{\text{HBr}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br}\)
Step 2 — make the alkoxide from 3-methylpentan-2-ol:
\(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}(\text{OH})-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{Na} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3-\text{CH}(\text{ONa})-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \tfrac{1}{2}\text{H}_2\)
Step 3 — couple them:
\(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}(\text{ONa})-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3-\text{CH}(\text{OC}_2\text{H}_5)-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{NaBr}\)

The opposite combination (sodium ethoxide with the secondary 2-halo-3-methylpentane) would fail, because the alkoxide would act as a base and eliminate, giving an alkene instead of the ether.

Set **(ii)**, sodium 4-nitrophenoxide with bromomethane, is the appropriate pair.

Williamson synthesis proceeds by \(\text{S}_\text{N}2\) attack of the alkoxide/phenoxide on the carbon of the halide. In set (ii) that carbon belongs to \(\text{CH}_3\text{Br}\), a primary (methyl) halide, which is ideal for \(\text{S}_\text{N}2\):
\(p\text{-O}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-ONa} + \text{CH}_3\text{Br} \rightarrow p\text{-O}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-OCH}_3 + \text{NaBr}\)

In set (i) the halogen sits on an aromatic ring. That carbon is \(sp^2\) hybridised and the C\(-\)Br bond has partial double-bond character through resonance, so it is shorter and stronger and cannot be attacked from the rear; an aryl halide does not undergo \(\text{S}_\text{N}2\). Set (i) is therefore not a Williamson synthesis.
_note: Strictly, 4-bromonitrobenzene does react with methoxide by nucleophilic AROMATIC substitution (addition-elimination), because the para nitro group stabilises the intermediate carbanion. That is a different mechanism from the SN2 of Williamson synthesis, and it is not the route the chapter teaches, so (ii) remains the appropriate answer to the question as asked.

solution:
Ethers are cleaved by hydrogen halides; the halide ion attacks the **less hindered** carbon by \(\text{S}_\text{N}2\), unless one group can form a stable carbocation, in which case \(\text{S}_\text{N}1\) operates at that carbon.
(i) Both groups are primary, so iodide/bromide attacks the smaller methyl group:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2-\text{O}-\text{CH}_3 + \text{HBr} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{Br} + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\)
(ii) In an aryl alkyl ether the aryl\(-\)O bond has partial double-bond character and the \(sp^2\) carbon cannot undergo nucleophilic substitution, so cleavage occurs at the alkyl\(-\)O bond:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{OC}_2\text{H}_5 + \text{HBr} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Br}\)
(iii) The ethoxy group is electron releasing by resonance and directs the electrophile to the ortho and para positions:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{OC}_2\text{H}_5 \xrightarrow[\text{conc. HNO}_3]{\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4}\) 1-ethoxy-2-nitrobenzene (minor) + 1-ethoxy-4-nitrobenzene (major).
(iv) The tert-butyl group gives a stable tertiary carbocation, so the reaction follows \(\text{S}_\text{N}1\) and the iodide ends up on the tertiary carbon:
\((\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{OC}_2\text{H}_5 + \text{HI} \rightarrow (\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{I} + \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}\)

(i) **2,2,4-Trimethylpentan-3-ol** (the \(-\text{OH}\) is on C-3 whichever end the pentane chain is numbered from, so the tie is broken by the substituent locants: numbering from the \(\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_2\) end gives \(\{2,2,4\}\), which is lower than \(\{2,4,4\}\) at the second point of difference)
(ii) **5-Ethylheptane-2,4-diol**
(iii) **Butane-2,3-diol**
(iv) **Propane-1,2,3-triol** (glycerol)
(v) **2-Methylphenol**
(vi) **4-Methylphenol**
(vii) **2,5-Dimethylphenol** (the set of locants \(\{2,5\}\) is lower than \(\{3,6\}\) obtained by numbering the other way)
(viii) **2,6-Dimethylphenol**
(ix) **1-Methoxy-2-methylpropane**
(x) **Ethoxybenzene**
(xi) **1-Phenoxyheptane**
(xii) **2-Ethoxybutane**

(i) 2-Methylbutan-2-ol: \(\text{CH}_3-\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)(\text{OH})-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3\)
(ii) 1-Phenylpropan-2-ol: \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}(\text{OH})-\text{CH}_3\)
(iii) 3,5-Dimethylhexane-1,3,5-triol: \(\text{HOCH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)(\text{OH})-\text{CH}_2-\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)(\text{OH})-\text{CH}_3\)
(iv) 2,3-Diethylphenol: a benzene ring with \(-\text{OH}\) at C-1 and \(-\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\) at C-2 and C-3
(v) 1-Ethoxypropane: \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5-\text{O}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\)
(vi) 2-Ethoxy-3-methylpentane: \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}(\text{OC}_2\text{H}_5)-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3\)
(vii) Cyclohexylmethanol: \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\)
(viii) 3-Cyclohexylpentan-3-ol: \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2-\text{C}(\text{OH})(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{11})-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\)
(ix) Cyclopent-3-en-1-ol: a cyclopentene ring with \(-\text{OH}\) at C-1 and the double bond between C-3 and C-4
(x) 4-Chloro-3-ethylbutan-1-ol: \(\text{HOCH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)-\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}\)
_note: The name in part (x) is not a correct IUPAC name for the structure it describes: taking the ethyl branch into the chain gives a five-carbon parent, so the same compound is properly named 3-(chloromethyl)pentan-1-ol. The structure asked for is nevertheless unambiguous and is the one drawn above.

solution:
[Textbook answer-key error: the key lists EIGHT lettered isomers of \(\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}\text{O}\) but they cover only SEVEN distinct compounds, and pentan-2-ol is missing. Entry (e) is printed as \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{OH}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3\), with the \(-\text{OH}\) inserted INTO the chain — impossible as written, since oxygen there would be divalent in a carbon chain — and it is then labelled pentan-3-ol, which is already entry (d). The argument closes rather than merely suggesting: there are exactly eight straight- and branched-chain alcohols of this formula, the key names eight, two of its names are the same compound, so exactly one is absent, and enumerating them identifies it as pentan-2-ol. All eight are listed below. (The key also leaves part (ii) of this question unanswered.)] (i) There are eight isomeric alcohols of formula \(\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}\text{O}\):
1. \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\) — Pentan-1-ol
2. \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_3\) — Pentan-2-ol
3. \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\) — Pentan-3-ol
4. \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\) — 2-Methylbutan-1-ol
5. \((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\) — 3-Methylbutan-1-ol
6. \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{OH}\) — 2-Methylbutan-2-ol
7. \((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_3\) — 3-Methylbutan-2-ol
8. \((\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\) — 2,2-Dimethylpropan-1-ol

(ii) Classifying by the number of carbons attached to the carbinol carbon:
Primary — 1, 4, 5 and 8;
Secondary — 2, 3 and 7;
Tertiary — 6.

Propan-1-ol \((M = 60)\) and butane \((M = 58)\) have almost the same molecular mass, so the dispersion forces available to them are comparable. Propanol, however, carries an \(-\text{O}-\text{H}\) bond: the large electronegativity difference makes the hydrogen strongly positive and the oxygen strongly negative, so propanol molecules associate through **intermolecular hydrogen bonds** \(\text{O}-\text{H}\cdots\text{O}\). Butane, a hydrocarbon, has no such polar bond and its molecules are held only by weak van der Waals forces.

Boiling requires the intermolecular attractions to be overcome, and breaking hydrogen bonds costs far more energy than breaking dispersion forces. Hence propanol boils at a much higher temperature than butane.

Dissolving a solute in water requires the water\(-\)water hydrogen bonds that are broken to be replaced by comparable solute\(-\)water interactions.

An alcohol has an \(-\text{OH}\) group that can act both as a hydrogen-bond **donor** (through its O\(-\)H hydrogen) and as an **acceptor** (through the lone pairs on oxygen), so it forms hydrogen bonds with water molecules, \(\text{R}-\text{O}-\text{H}\cdots\text{OH}_2\). The energy released compensates for the disruption of water's own hydrogen-bonded network, so the alcohol dissolves.

A hydrocarbon of comparable molecular mass is non-polar and can neither donate nor accept a hydrogen bond. It can only break up water's hydrogen bonding without offering anything in return, so it is essentially insoluble. (The solubility of alcohols falls as the alkyl group gets larger, because the hydrophobic part then outweighs the hydrogen-bonding \(-\text{OH}\) group.)

Hydroboration-oxidation is a two-stage conversion of an alkene into an alcohol. First diborane adds across the double bond to give a trialkylborane; the boron atom becomes attached to the \(sp^2\) carbon that carries the **greater** number of hydrogen atoms. The trialkylborane is then oxidised by hydrogen peroxide in aqueous alkali, each C\(-\)B bond being replaced by C\(-\)OH with retention of position.

Example, with propene:
\(3\,\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2 + (\text{BH}_3)_2 \rightarrow 2\,(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2)_3\text{B}\)
\((\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2)_3\text{B} \xrightarrow[\text{OH}^-]{3\text{H}_2\text{O}_2} 3\,\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH} + \text{B(OH)}_3\)

The overall result is addition of water **against** Markovnikov's rule — the \(-\text{OH}\) ends up on the less substituted carbon — and propan-1-ol, not propan-2-ol, is obtained, in excellent yield.

A monohydric phenol must have the \(-\text{OH}\) group attached directly to the benzene ring. With \(\text{C}_7\text{H}_8\text{O}\) the remaining carbon is a ring methyl group, so the three isomers are the cresols:

1. \(o\)-Cresol — a benzene ring with \(-\text{OH}\) at C-1 and \(-\text{CH}_3\) at C-2: **2-Methylphenol**
2. \(m\)-Cresol — \(-\text{OH}\) at C-1 and \(-\text{CH}_3\) at C-3: **3-Methylphenol**
3. \(p\)-Cresol — \(-\text{OH}\) at C-1 and \(-\text{CH}_3\) at C-4: **4-Methylphenol**

The other two compounds of this formula are excluded: benzyl alcohol \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\) is an alcohol (its \(-\text{OH}\) is on an \(sp^3\) carbon) and anisole \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OCH}_3\) is an ether.

The **ortho** isomer is steam volatile.

In \(o\)-nitrophenol the \(-\text{OH}\) group and the \(-\text{NO}_2\) group are on adjacent carbons and are correctly placed to form an **intramolecular** hydrogen bond, closing a six-membered chelate ring. The \(-\text{OH}\) hydrogen is thus used up within the same molecule, so the molecules cannot associate with one another; the substance remains effectively monomeric, has a low boiling point and distils over with steam.

In \(p\)-nitrophenol the two groups are far apart, so the hydrogen bonding must be **intermolecular**. The molecules become associated into larger aggregates, which raises the energy needed to vaporise them; \(p\)-nitrophenol is therefore much less volatile and stays behind in the flask. This difference is the basis of the separation.

Cumene (isopropylbenzene) is oxidised by air at the benzylic C\(-\)H bond to cumene hydroperoxide, and the hydroperoxide is then decomposed by dilute acid to phenol and propanone:

Step 1: \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2 + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_2-\text{O}-\text{O}-\text{H}\)
(cumene \(\rightarrow\) cumene hydroperoxide)

Step 2: \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_2-\text{O}-\text{O}-\text{H} \xrightarrow[\text{H}_2\text{O}]{\text{H}^+} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + \text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3\)

The benzylic position is attacked because the tertiary benzylic radical formed there is resonance stabilised. Propanone (acetone) is obtained as a valuable by-product, which is why this is the route used for most of the world's phenol.

Chlorobenzene is an aryl halide, so its C\(-\)Cl bond is strong and resists nucleophilic substitution; very forcing conditions are needed. It is fused with sodium hydroxide at about 623 K under a pressure of some 300 atmospheres, giving sodium phenoxide, which is then acidified:

\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl} + \text{NaOH} \xrightarrow[300\ \text{atm}]{623\ \text{K}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{ONa} + \text{HCl}\)
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{ONa} + \text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + \text{NaCl}\)

The product is phenol.

The hydration of ethene is an acid-catalysed electrophilic addition and takes place in three steps.

**Step 1 — protonation of the alkene.** The \(\pi\) electrons of ethene attack a proton supplied by \(\text{H}_3\text{O}^+\), giving a carbocation:
\(\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2 + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+ \rightarrow \text{CH}_3-\overset{+}{\text{C}}\text{H}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)

**Step 2 — nucleophilic attack of water on the carbocation.** A lone pair on the oxygen of water attacks the electron-deficient carbon:
\(\text{CH}_3-\overset{+}{\text{C}}\text{H}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\overset{+}{\text{O}}\text{H}_2\)

**Step 3 — deprotonation.** Another water molecule removes a proton from the oxonium ion, regenerating the catalyst:
\(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\overset{+}{\text{O}}\text{H}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH} + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+\)

The product is ethanol, and the proton consumed in step 1 is returned in step 3, so the acid is a true catalyst.

Benzene is first sulphonated, the sulphonic acid group is then displaced by \(-\text{OH}\) using molten alkali, and the sodium salt is finally acidified.

Step 1 — sulphonation with concentrated sulphuric acid (oleum):
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_6 + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{SO}_3\text{H} + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)
(benzenesulphonic acid)

Step 2 — heating with molten sodium hydroxide:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{SO}_3\text{H} + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{ONa} + \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)
(sodium phenoxide)

Step 3 — acidification:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{ONa} + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + \text{Na}^+\)

The product is phenol.
